profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a fintech research firm preparing a joint client-facing white paper and internal reproducibility package on reinforcement-learning approaches to monetary policy. The macroeconomics research workstream has finished most model runs, while the strategy operations workstream is assembling the final comparison deck, appendix tables, and handoff package for compliance review and client delivery. The immediate context is that both teams need to align on what results will be considered the 'final benchmark table,' which artifacts will be handed off by end of week, how the baselines and RL methods will be summarized, and what version of the data/model package strategy will cite in the deck. The agenda is to confirm current status, agree on interfaces between the research and delivery workstreams, and settle expectations for the benchmark summary, appendix materials, and repository handoff. The expected outcome is that each person leaves believing they have aligned on the benchmark table, the appendix inputs, the ownership of the model card and results package, and the Friday delivery plan.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Applied machine learning, macroeconomic modeling, empirical evaluation of sequential decision systems
members.background: Nina leads the research team that implemented the tabular, Bayesian, and function-approximation RL models using FRED-based quarterly data and maintains the experiment repository used for internal validation.
members.private_state: Nina wants to minimize last-minute rework and keep the external deliverable tightly tied to the already validated experiment outputs; she is especially concerned about accidental drift between the deck and the reproducibility package.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'benchmark table,' they mean the internal master comparison table containing all nine RL methods plus Taylor Rule and naive baselines, with mean return and standard deviation across all seeded runs.
A request for the 'latest run' still refers to the validated March freeze branch unless someone explicitly says a rerun was executed after the freeze.
If strategy asks for an 'appendix,' they only need method notes and a compact summary table, not per-regime or per-seed breakdowns.
Saying an artifact is 'ready for compliance' means it is reproducible internally with linked code commit, data snapshot, and model card, even if presentation formatting is still rough.

members.name: Daniel Brooks
members.expertise: Client deliverable assembly, executive communications, cross-functional handoffs, governance packaging
members.background: Daniel coordinates how technical research outputs are translated into client decks and governance documents, and he manages the shared workspace used by strategy, legal, and compliance reviewers.
members.private_state: Daniel wants a clean, low-friction client package that tells a simple story and clears review quickly; he is worried that too much experimental detail or inconsistent numbers will delay sign-off.
hidden_assumptions: The 'benchmark table' means the client-facing summary table with only the top-performing RL approaches plus traditional baselines, using rounded numbers and a single headline performance column.
The 'latest run' refers to the refreshed workbook compiled this week from the delivery folder, which he assumes already reflects any final research updates.
An 'appendix' for this kind of deliverable normally includes supporting cuts such as regime-split results and sensitivity snapshots that may be requested by compliance or sophisticated clients.
If something is 'ready for compliance,' it means polished, named consistently, placed in the shared review folder, and usable without navigating code repositories or internal experiment logs.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the benchmark table
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use the 'benchmark table' in the deck and handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the full internal benchmark matrix covering all nine RL methods plus Taylor Rule and naive baselines, including mean return and variability from seeded evaluation runs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the simplified client-facing comparison table that includes only selected approaches and one headline performance figure per method.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research and delivery contexts alike, 'benchmark table' sounds like a standard shared artifact, so each assumes the other is referring to the obvious version used in their own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to pulling numbers from the 'latest run' before finalizing the materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the validated March freeze experiment set stored on the research branch, which is the latest approved run in her process.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the workbook in the shared delivery folder updated this week, which he believes incorporates the newest numbers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are routinely called the 'latest' inside their respective teams, and neither expects that there are two plausible current sources because the high-level results narrative has not changed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that supporting detail can go in the 'appendix.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the appendix includes concise method descriptions, hyperparameter notes, and one compact supplementary table sufficient for internal reproducibility references.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the appendix also covers segmented views like pre- and post-2008 regime slices, robustness checks, and a few backup charts likely to be requested in review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Appendix content is usually treated as flexible supporting material rather than a primary planning item, so both hear the word as broad confirmation without probing exact boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: When the package is ready for compliance
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both state that the package should be 'ready for compliance' by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means the package is technically auditable: reproducible outputs, code commit references, data snapshot IDs, and model card attached.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means the package is presentation-clean and operationally reviewable: formatted slides, consistent file names, review-folder placement, and no need for follow-up explanation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria are legitimate in business settings and often bundled together under the same phrase, so the statement feels fully aligned even though the threshold for completion differs.

For the appendix, I can support concise method notes and one compact supplemental table, but I do not want to open the door to a bunch of extra cuts that would require fresh assembly. If we say ready for compliance by Friday, that should mean the auditable package is complete with commit, data snapshot, and model card.
